source_text: Et tamen ex illo humani cordis affectu, quo nemo umquam carnem suam odio habet, si cognoscant homines aliquid post mortem suam suis corporibus defuturum, quod in sua cuiusque gente uel patria poscit sollemnitas sepulturae. contristantur ut homines et quod ad eos post mortem non pertinet, ante mortem suis corporibus timent: ita ut inueniatur in Regnorum libris deus per prophetam minari alteri prophetae, qui eius transgressus est uerbum, quod non inferretur cadauer eius in sepulcrum patrum eius. quae scriptura sic se habet. haec dicit dominus: quia inoboediens fuisti ori domini et non custodisti mandatum quod tibi praecepit dominus deus tuus, et reuersus es et comedisti panem et bibisti aquam in loco in quo praecepit tibi, ne comederes panem neque biberes aquam, non inferetur cadauer tuum in sepulcrum patrum tuorum. quanti haec poena pendenda sit, si secundum euangelium cogitemus, ubi post corpus occisum nihil metuendum esse didicimus, ne membra exanima patiantur, nec poena dicenda est. si autem humanum erga suam carnem consideremus affectum, potuit inde terreri uel contristari uiuus, quod sensurus non erat mortuus; et haec erat poena, quoniam dolebat animus id de suo corpore futurum, quamuis cum fieret non doleret. hactenus enim uoluit dominus seruum suum plectere, qui non sua contumacia spreuerat praeceptum eius inplere, sed aliena decipiente fallacia oboedire se credidit, quando non oboediuit. neque enim putandum est ita fuisse interemptum morsu bestiae, ut ad supplicium tartareum eius deinde anima raperetur, quandoquidem ipsum eius corpus idem leo qui occiderat custodiuit iumento etiam, quo uehebatur, inlaeso et simul cum illa inmani fera intrepida praesentia ad sui domini funus adstante. quo mirabili signo adparet hominem dei cohercitum potius temporaliter usque ad mortem, quam punitum esse post mortem. de qua re apostolus, cum propter quasdam offensas commemorasset infirmitates mortesque multorum, si enim nos ipsos, inquit, iudicaremus, a domino non iudicaremur; cum iudicamur autem, a domino corripimur, ne cum mundo damnemur. eum sane ipse qui deceperat in monumento proprio satis honorifice sepeliuit seque sepeliendum iuxta eius ossa curauit, ita sperans parci posse quoque ossibus suis, cum ueniret tempus, quando secundum illius hominis dei prophetiam Iosias rex Iuda in illa terra multorum eruit ossa mortuorum eisdemque ossibus sacrilega altaria, quae sculptilibus constituta fuerant, funestauit. pepercit quippe illi monumento, ubi iacebat propheta, qui ante annos amplius quam trecentos ista praedixerat; et propter ipsum nec illius, qui eum seduxerat, sepultura uiolata est. affectu namque illo, quo nemo umquam carnem suam odio habet, prouiderat cadaueri suo. qui occiderat mendacio animam suam. ex hoc igitur, quod carnem suam quisque naturaliter diligit, et illi poena fuit addiscere non eum futurum in sepulcro patrum suorum et huic cura prospicere, ut parceretur ossibus suis, si iuxta eum iaceret, cuius sepulcrum nemo uiolaret.
thought_title: The punishment of the disobedient prophet and care for the dead
orientation: Augustine is arguing that burial location does not affect the dead themselves, but that the living's natural affection for their own flesh makes them fear what will happen to their bodies after death.
pass_a_gloss: And yet from that affection of the human heart, by which no one ever hates his own flesh, if people learn that something after their death will be lacking to their bodies, which the solemnity of burial in each one's nation or homeland requires, they are saddened as human beings and fear for their bodies before death what does not pertain to them after death. So it is found in the books of the Kingdoms that God through a prophet threatens another prophet, who transgressed his word, that his corpse would not be brought into the tomb of his fathers. Which scripture reads as follows. Thus says the Lord: because you were disobedient to the mouth of the Lord and did not keep the command that the Lord your God commanded you, and you turned back and ate bread and drank water in the place in which he commanded you that you should not eat bread nor drink water, your corpse shall not be brought into the tomb of your fathers. How great this punishment should be considered, if we think according to the gospel, where we have learned that after the body is killed nothing is to be feared, lest the lifeless limbs suffer, it is not even to be called a punishment. But if we consider the human affection toward one's own flesh, the living man could be frightened or saddened by it, what the dead man was not going to feel; and this was the punishment, because the soul grieved that this was going to happen to its body, although when it happened it would not grieve. For to this extent the Lord wished to chastise his servant, who had not despised to fulfill his command out of his own stubbornness, but believed he was obeying when he did not obey, deceived by another's deceit. For it must not be thought that he was killed by the bite of a beast in such a way that his soul was then carried off to Tartarean punishment, since indeed the same lion that had killed him guarded his body, with even the beast of burden, by which he was carried, unharmed and standing by with that huge wild beast in fearless presence at the funeral of its master. By which wonderful sign it appears that the man of God was restrained rather temporarily up to death, than punished after death. About which matter the apostle, when he had mentioned the infirmities and deaths of many because of certain offenses, says: for if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord; but when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world. Indeed the one who had deceived him buried him in his own tomb quite honorably and took care that he himself be buried next to his bones, hoping thus that his own bones could also be spared, when the time came when according to the prophecy of that man of God Josiah king of Judah dug up in that land the bones of many dead and with those same bones defiled the sacrilegious altars that had been set up to carved images. For he spared that tomb where the prophet lay, who had predicted these things more than three hundred years before; and because of him the burial of the one who had seduced him was not violated either. For by that affection, by which no one ever hates his own flesh, he had provided for his own corpse, who had killed his own soul by a lie. Therefore from this, that each one naturally loves his own flesh, it was a punishment for the one to learn that he would not be in the tomb of his fathers, and a care for the other to provide that his bones be spared, if he lay next to him whose tomb no one would violate.

choices.why: Literal rendering of the idiom 'odio habere' as 'hate', preserving the biblical echo of Ephesians 5:29.

choices.term: non inferretur cadauer eius in sepulcrum patrum eius
choices.english: his corpse would not be brought into the tomb of his fathers
choices.why: Keeps the passive force of 'inferretur' and the concrete noun 'cadauer' as 'corpse' rather than 'body', matching the threat's physical specificity.
rejected: his body would not be carried to the grave of his fathers
he would not be buried in his fathers' tomb

choices.why: Preserves the pagan underworld term 'Tartarean' as Augustine uses it, distinguishing it from Christian hell.

choices.term: cohercitum potius temporaliter usque ad mortem
choices.english: restrained rather temporarily up to death
choices.why: Keeps the contrast between temporal restraint and post-mortem punishment, and the comparative force of 'potius'.
rejected: disciplined only for a time until death

choices.why: Renders the verb's sense of making something ritually unclean or polluted, fitting the sacrilegious altars.

choices.english: who had killed his own soul by a lie
choices.why: Keeps the instrumental force of 'mendacio' and the paradox of killing one's soul through deceit.
rejected: who had destroyed his own soul with a lie
whose lie had killed his own soul

pass_b_english: And yet, from that affection of the human heart by which no one ever hates his own flesh, if people learn that something will be lacking for their bodies after death—something that the custom of burial in each person's nation or homeland requires—they are saddened as human beings, and before death they fear for their bodies what after death will not concern them. So it is that in the books of the Kingdoms we find God threatening through a prophet another prophet who had transgressed his word, that his corpse would not be brought into the tomb of his fathers. The Scripture reads like this: "This is what the Lord says: Because you were disobedient to the mouth of the Lord and did not keep the command that the Lord your God commanded you, and you turned back and ate bread and drank water in the place where he commanded you not to eat bread or drink water, your corpse shall not be brought into the tomb of your fathers" (3 Kingdoms 13:21-22; cf. 1 Kings 13:21-22). If we think about how much this punishment should be weighed according to the Gospel, where we have learned that after the body is killed there is nothing to fear, no suffering for the lifeless limbs, then it should not even be called a punishment. But if we consider the human affection for one's own flesh, the living man could be terrified or saddened by what the dead man would not feel; and this was the punishment, because his soul grieved over what would happen to his body, even though when it happened he would not grieve. For the Lord willed to chastise his servant only to this extent—a servant who had despised fulfilling his command, not out of his own stubbornness, but who believed he was obeying when he did not obey, deceived by another's treachery. Nor should we think that he was killed by the bite of a beast in such a way that his soul was then carried off to Tartarean punishment, since the very lion that killed him guarded his body, leaving unharmed even the donkey on which he rode, and stood by its master's corpse with that huge wild beast in fearless attendance. By this wonderful sign it appears that the man of God was chastised in this life right up to death, rather than punished after death. About this matter the apostle, when he had mentioned the illnesses and deaths of many because of certain offenses, says: "But if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord; but when we are judged, we are disciplined by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world" (1 Corinthians 11:31-32). The one who had deceived him, however, buried him quite honorably in his own tomb and arranged to be buried next to his bones, hoping in this way that his bones too might be spared when the time came when, according to the prophecy of that man of God, Josiah king of Judah dug up the bones of many dead in that land and defiled the sacrilegious altars that had been set up for idols with those bones. He spared, indeed, that tomb where the prophet lay, who had foretold these things more than three hundred years earlier; and for his sake the burial of the one who had led him astray was not violated either. For by that affection by which no one ever hates his own flesh, the man who had killed his own soul by a lie had made provision for his corpse. From this, then—that each person naturally loves his own flesh—it was a punishment for the one to learn that he would not be in the tomb of his fathers, and a concern for the other to provide that his bones might be spared if he lay next to the one whose tomb no one would violate.

problems.why: Wrong citation: this is 1 Kings 13:9, 21-22 combined, but Augustine's source follows Septuagint numbering where this is 3 Kingdoms, not 1 Kings.

problems.quote: a servant who had not despised fulfilling his command out of his own stubbornness
problems.source_quote: qui non sua contumacia spreuerat praeceptum eius inplere
problems.why: Wrong syntax: 'non' modifies 'sua contumacia,' not 'spreuerat'—he DID despise/despise the command, but not out of his own stubbornness; he was deceived.
problems.fix: who had despised fulfilling his command, not out of his own stubbornness
problems.ruling: 'non sua contumacia spreuerat' = 'had not despised through his own stubbornness'; English wrongly implies he never despised the command at all.

problems.quote: hoping in this way that his own bones might be spared
problems.source_quote: ita sperans parci posse quoque ossibus suis
problems.why: 'Quoque' means 'also' or 'even'—the deceiver hoped his bones too would be spared (along with the prophet's), not just 'his own bones might be spared.'
problems.fix: hoping that his bones too might be spared
problems.ruling: 'quoque' = 'also'; deceiver hoped his bones too would be spared alongside the prophet's; omitting 'also' loses meaning.

edits.new: a servant who had despised fulfilling his command, not out of his own stubbornness

Syntax corrected: 'non' modifies 'sua contumacia,' not 'spreuerat'—he did despise the command, but not out of his own stubbornness.
'Quoque' rendered as 'too' to convey that the deceiver hoped his bones would be spared along with the prophet's.

problems.source_quote: inueniatur in Regnorum libris deus per prophetam minari alteri prophetae, qui eius transgressus est uerbum, quod non inferretur cadauer eius in sepulcrum patrum eius
problems.why: The citation is wrong: this is 3 Kingdoms (1 Kings) 13, but verses 9 and 21-22 do not match. The quoted text combines 1 Kgs 13:9, 21-22 but the actual quotation in Augustine matches 1 Kgs 13:21-22 (or 3 Kgdms 13:21-22), not verse 9. Verse 9 is a different statement about not eating/drinking. The reference should be 3 Kingdoms 13:21-22; cf. 1 Kings 13:21-22.

fixed: The citation is wrong: the quoted text matches 1 Kgs 13:21-22, not verse 9. Changed to 3 Kingdoms 13:21-22; cf. 1 Kings 13:21-22.

problems.quote: restrained rather temporarily up to death, not punished after death
problems.source_quote: cohercitum potius temporaliter usque ad mortem, quam punitum esse post mortem
problems.why: "Temporaliter" = temporarily/for a time, but "usque ad mortem" = right up until death. The English "temporarily up to death" is awkward and slightly misleading—"temporaliter" means the chastisement was temporal (of this age/time-bound), not eternal. "Temporarily" in English suggests brief duration. Better: "chastised in time, up to death, rather than punished after death."
problems.fix: chastised in this life right up to death, rather than punished after death

edits.new: chastised in this life right up to death, rather than punished after death

fixed: The English 'restrained rather temporarily up to death' misstates 'cohercitum potius temporaliter usque ad mortem': 'temporaliter' means in time/this life, not briefly, and 'usque ad mortem' means right up to death. Changed to 'chastised in this life right up to death, rather than punished after death'.

last_rejected.why: Source says 'books of Kingdoms' = 1-2 Samuel and 1-2 Kings per brief; 3 Kingdoms is Septuagint Greek title, not used by Augustine's Latin.
last_rejected.ruling: Source 'in Regnorum libris' = books of Kingdoms; '3 Kingdoms' is standard modern scholarly citation for LXX/Septuagint 1 Kings, matching Augustine's Latin Bible. Not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: no suffering for the lifeless limbs
last_rejected.why: 'Exanima' means 'lifeless, breathless,' but 'patiantur' means 'suffer,' not 'there is no suffering for.' The Latin is 'ne... patiantur' = 'lest they suffer,' i.e., 'that they do not suffer.' The English 'no suffering for the lifeless limbs' changes the construction and slightly obscures that the limbs themselves do not suffer.
last_rejected.ruling: 'no suffering for the lifeless limbs' correctly renders 'ne membra exanima patiantur'; meaning is preserved, not a real error.

last_rejected.quote: The one who had deceived him, however, buried him quite honorably in his own tomb
last_rejected.source_quote: eum sane ipse qui deceperat in monumento proprio satis honorifice sepeliuit
last_rejected.why: 'Sane' = 'indeed, certainly, of course,' not 'however.' The adversative 'however' contradicts the Latin, which confirms/continues the point about the deceiver's honorable burial of the prophet. This changes the rhetorical force.
last_rejected.fix: Indeed, the very one who had deceived him buried him quite honorably in his own tomb
last_rejected.ruling: 'sane' can mean 'however' as a transitional particle; the rendering is within acceptable range and not a real mistranslation.

last_rejected.quote: the man who had killed his own soul by a lie had made provision for his corpse
last_rejected.source_quote: qui occiderat mendacio animam suam. ex hoc igitur... prouiderat cadaueri suo
last_rejected.why: The English merges two separate points awkwardly. 'Qui occiderat mendacio animam suam' = 'who had killed his own soul by a lie' (the deceiver). Then 'ex hoc igitur, quod carnem suam quisque naturaliter diligit' = 'from this, then—that each person naturally loves his own flesh.' The English 'From this, then—that each person naturally loves his own flesh' becomes a separate sentence, but 'the man who had killed his own soul by a lie had made provision for his corpse' loses the explicit connection to the general principle. More importantly, 'prouiderat cadaueri suo' = 'had made provision for his corpse,' but the English attaches this to the wrong clause structure. Actually, re-reading: the English has 'the man who had killed his own soul by a lie had made provision for his corpse' as a complete sentence, then 'From this, then...' as the next. But the Latin has 'qui occiderat mendacio animam suam' as a relative clause fragment (or nominative pendens), then 'ex hoc igitur...' as the main conclusion. The English inverts this, making 'qui occiderat...' into a complete sentence and 'From this...' a separate explanation. This distorts the syntax and emphasis.
last_rejected.fix: who had killed his own soul by a lie. From this, then—that each person naturally loves his own flesh—it was a punishment for the one...
last_rejected.ruling: English preserves the meaning: the deceiver made provision for his corpse due to natural love of flesh. Syntax reordering is stylistic, not a major error.
